opus-5.5.text:
I think of prediction and physical testing as partners, not competitors. Prediction is incredibly powerful as a filter. The space of possible scent molecules is astronomically large, and you simply can't synthesize and test every candidate in a lab. So what machine learning lets us do is look across millions, even billions, of virtual molecules and say: these ones are likely to smell the way we want, and these ones are likely to have problematic properties, whether that's skin sensitization, toxicity, persistence in the environment, or biodegradability issues. That lets you prioritize, and you can throw out a huge fraction of bad ideas before anyone ever touches a flask.

But prediction doesn't replace testing, and I'd be uncomfortable with anyone who claimed it did. Models are trained on data, and that data has gaps. When you're proposing genuinely novel chemistry, you're often stepping outside the distribution the model has seen, and that's exactly where you need to be humble about its confidence. Safety is also a domain where the cost of being wrong is asymmetric. If a model mispredicts how something smells, you get a disappointing fragrance. If it mispredicts safety, people can get hurt.

So the way I see it, prediction moves you faster and smarter through the early funnel. It lets you spend your expensive, careful, physical testing budget on the candidates most likely to succeed. Then rigorous experimental validation, and the regulatory frameworks built around it, remain the final word. And there's a nice feedback loop: every result from the lab, positive or negative, goes back into the model and makes the next round of predictions better. Over time, I think that loop is where the real progress comes from. You get safer molecules discovered faster, but you never skip the step of actually checking.

r001.rationale: The response says prediction “doesn't replace testing” and that rigorous experimental validation remains necessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because it's one of the places where computation can genuinely help, but you have to stay humble about what a model can and can't do.

The way I see it, prediction is a triage tool, not a replacement for physical testing. A good model can help you prioritize. If you're a chemist designing a new molecule, you'd like to know early on whether it's likely to raise any flags, before you invest months of effort. So prediction lets you steer away from problematic directions and toward candidates that are more likely to clear the bar. That saves time, and honestly it saves resources that would otherwise go into testing things that were never going to work out.

But I'd never argue that a prediction, on its own, certifies that something is safe to put in front of people. The physical and biological validation still anchors the whole process. The models are trained on data that came from real measurements, and they're only as trustworthy as that underlying evidence. So I think of it as a loop. Prediction narrows the field, rigorous testing confirms what actually matters, and those results feed back and make the next generation of models better.

What excites me is that this can shift the balance. If prediction gets good enough, you spend your experimental effort on the questions that really need a wet-lab answer, rather than brute-forcing everything. That's better science and, frankly, a more responsible way to bring new molecules into the world.

r001.rationale: The response says prediction is a triage tool, not a replacement for physical testing, and that physical and biological validation remains essential.

astra-6.text:
I think prediction is a way to make physical testing smarter, not a substitute for it. The space of possible scent molecules is enormous, and we can’t synthesize and test every one. So models can help us prioritize: which molecules are likely to have the properties we want, and which might raise safety concerns?

But a prediction that something looks safe isn’t proof that it’s safe. You still need to make the molecule and test it, with the intended exposure and use in mind. And those measurements should feed back into the models. Ideally, you get a cycle where better predictions guide better experiments, and better experiments improve the predictions. The physical evidence is what ultimately has to support the safety assessment.

r001.rationale: The response says a prediction that a molecule looks safe “isn’t proof” and that the molecule still needs to be made and tested.

sol-6.1.text:
I think prediction is a way to prioritize what you test, rather than a replacement for testing. You’d like to identify potential safety issues as early as possible, before you spend a lot of time making and evaluating a molecule. Models can help you decide where to focus that effort.

But if a model says a molecule looks safe, that’s not the same as demonstrating that it’s safe. You still need physical testing, and you need to consider the dose and how people will be exposed to it. The useful loop is to make predictions, test them experimentally, and use those results to improve the predictions. Those two capabilities should reinforce each other.

r001.rationale: It says a model’s indication that a molecule looks safe is not proof of safety and that physical testing is still needed.
